HAC Sandwich Variance of the Coefficients

Source: R/sandwich_hac.R
hac_sandwich.Rd

Select a heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent meat for the frequentist variance \(V = V_b B V_b\), with \(V_b = (H + S)^{-1}\) the inverse of the penalized information. Pass the object as the sandwich argument of frequentist_vcov(). It is the counterpart of hc0_sandwich() for dependent observations, and the estimator of Newey and West (1987) with the Bartlett kernel.

Usage

hac_sandwich(
  kernel = c("bartlett", "parzen", "truncated"),
  bandwidth = NULL,
  time = NULL,
  cluster = NULL,
  data = NULL
)

Arguments

kernel

"bartlett" (the default), "parzen" or "truncated".

bandwidth

NULL (the default), which takes \(\lfloor 4 (T/100)^{2/9} \rfloor\), or a non-negative whole number, the largest lag \(L\).

time

NULL (the default) or a one-sided formula with one variable, such as ~ t, for a model without a structural term.

cluster

NULL (the default) or a one-sided formula with one variable, such as ~ id, that separates the series of a model without a structural term.

data

NULL (the default) or the data frame that holds time and cluster, with one row for each observation of the fit.

Value

A HacSandwich object with the properties type ("HAC"), kernel, bandwidth, time, cluster and data.

Details

The score \(u_t\) of observation \(t\) is the derivative of its log-likelihood contribution in the whole vector of unknowns: the coefficients of every distribution parameter, and the own parameters of a structural term on the unconstrained scale. For a modelterms7::gas() term the contribution of \(t\) depends on the parameters through the filtered level, and \(u_t\) carries that dependence: it is the sum over the equations of the derivative of the log-density in the predictor, on the link scale, times the derivative of the predictor in the unknowns, which the forward recursion of the filter supplies. For a modelterms7::regime() term the contribution is the increment \(\log p(y_t \mid y_1, \dots, y_{t-1})\) of the forward recursion, and \(u_t\) its derivative, computed in forward mode through the recursion. In both cases \(\sum_t u_t\) is the gradient of the log-likelihood.

With a well specified filter the scores are martingale differences and \(B = \sum_t u_t u_t'\) already estimates their variance. The HAC meat adds the autocovariances, $$B = \Gamma_0 + \sum_{l=1}^{L} k\!\left(\frac{l}{L + 1}\right) (\Gamma_l + \Gamma_l'), \qquad \Gamma_l = \sum_t u_t u_{t-l}',$$ where \(k\) is the kernel and \(L\) the bandwidth, the largest lag. The Bartlett kernel is \(k(x) = 1 - x\), the Parzen kernel is \(1 - 6x^2 + 6x^3\) for \(x \le 1/2\) and \(2(1 - x)^3\) up to one, and the truncated kernel is one. With bandwidth = 0 the meat is \(\sum_t u_t u_t'\), the meat of hc0_sandwich(). No finite-sample correction is applied.

The default bandwidth is \(L = \lfloor 4 (T / 100)^{2/9} \rfloor\), with \(T\) the number of observations of a group (the mean number, when the groups differ in length). A bandwidth larger than the longest group minus one is reduced to that.

With a by in the structural term the series are panels. A lag runs within a group only, so the product of two scores of different groups enters no \(\Gamma_l\), and the groups are independent. Observations are ordered within a group as the structural term orders them (its time), and a lag is a step in that order, whatever the gaps between times.

A model without a structural term has no order of its own. time names the variable that orders the observations and cluster the variable that separates independent series; both are read from data, or from the data of the call to statmod(), which is evaluated again in the environment of the model formula. For a model with a structural term they are not accepted, since the term fixes the order and the groups.

The prior weights of statmod() multiply the log-likelihood contribution of an observation, and so its score; they are not otherwise interpreted. A model with a term whose block moves with its coefficients is accepted when hc0_sandwich() accepts it: the scores are those of the block read at the fit, and a frozen working linearization of a sharp step is rejected.

References

Newey, W. K. and West, K. D. (1987). A simple, positive semi-definite, heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix. Econometrica, 55(3), 703–708.

See also

frequentist_vcov(), which takes the object, and hc0_sandwich() for independent observations.

Examples

set.seed(1)
n <- 120
dd <- data.frame(t = seq_len(n), x = rnorm(n))
e <- as.numeric(stats::filter(rnorm(n), 0.6, method = "recursive"))
dd$y <- 1 + 0.5 * dd$x + e
fit <- statmod(y ~ x, distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), dd)
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, vcov_type = frequentist_vcov(
  sandwich = hc0_sandwich()))))[1:2]
#> mu:(Intercept)           mu:x 
#>      0.1152153      0.1236192 
sqrt(diag(vcov(fit, vcov_type = frequentist_vcov(
  sandwich = hac_sandwich(time = ~ t)))))[1:2]
#> mu:(Intercept)           mu:x 
#>      0.1894405      0.1017458
